newsitem.title: GERMANY: German beef sales plummet on latest BSE fears.
newsitem.headline: German beef sales plummet on latest BSE fears.

text.p: German beef sales are dropping sharply on new fears of mad cow disease, the central farm marketing and price office ZMP said on Thursday.

Export chances to Russia were uncertain because in Russian terms, Germany was technically no longer entirely free of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), a ZMP market report for the week ending February 2 said.
Slaughter rates and prices should fall in the weeks to come.
Beef sales in the Hamburg meat market dropped by 20 to 50 percent this week. Both buying-in and resale prices were down and conditions were similar in the Berlin and Cologne markets.
German operators anticipating lower meat demand reduced slaughter rates of young bulls by up to 70 percent.
Average quality male beef ex-producer was put at 5.00 marks per kg, down from 5.19 marks in the week ended January 26 and compared with 5.35 marks a year ago.
Germany on January 21 confirmed the first case of a calf believed to have been born in the country to die of BSE and the death of a woman, possibly from BSE-related brain disease.
The calf could have been infected by its mother, which was imported from Britain.
German beef consumption had just barely recovered from a slump prompted by a British announcement last year that a likely link had been established between BSE and its fatal human equivalent, CJD.
Per-capita beef consumption in 1996 dropped by one kg to 10.3 kg as consumers preferred pork, lamb and poultry.
German exports to central and eastern European countries have now virtually stopped and trade with other EU countries such as France and Denmark has also been reduced, ZMP said.
